Case 01

KudiPay Security Incident — Full Breach Investigation

Wireshark Kali Linux CLI (grep/awk) Firewall syslog analysis Formal incident reporting
Scenario

A mentorship capstone (with The Victor Akinode Initiatives) simulating a real-world breach against a fintech company, "KudiPay." The brief: reconstruct the full attack chain from network evidence and produce a formal incident report.

Method

Filtered and analyzed firewall syslogs on a Kali Linux VM using grep and awk to isolate RDP (port 3389) traffic, cross-referenced against a Wireshark packet capture of the same environment to confirm session behavior and DNS activity.

1/2
Firewall perimeter syslog — filtering allowed traffic on the KudiPay network
Continued log review — identifying the pattern later confirmed as lateral RDP movement
← swipe for 2 images →
Packet Capture (Wireshark)
Packet capture — DNS query to a suspicious external domain, followed by RDP traffic
Attack chain reconstructed

Web application exploitation (likely injection-based) → internal reconnaissance → suspicious DNS query to data-sync.exfil-node.net → lateral movement via internal RDP → outbound RDP session to an external IP, transferring 29,825 bytes.

Risk assessment
Confidentiality
HIGH
Integrity
MEDIUM
Availability
NO IMPACT
Finding

The breach could have been prevented at a single low-cost control point: outbound traffic restriction, specifically egress filtering on RDP and DNS. No individual layer failed catastrophically — the attacker moved undetected by blending into normal-looking traffic across layers that were only monitored in isolation, not correlated.

Case 02

RDP Brute-Force Attack & Log Correlation

Windows Event Viewer Excel — log timeline
Scenario

A simulated environment showed repeated failed logon attempts against a privileged "finance-admin" account over RDP (port 3389), originating from an external IP.

Method

Built a timeline in Excel correlating firewall connection logs with Windows Security event logs — tracking failed logon attempts (Event ID 4625) through to the successful breach (Event ID 4624), then the attacker's follow-on activity.

Correlated log timeline — 10 failed attempts followed by a successful brute-force breach
Verification in Event Viewer
1/2
Event ID 4624 — successful logon events filtered in Security log
Event ID 5379 — Credential Manager credentials read, flagged for follow-up
← swipe for 2 images →
Finding

After 10 failed attempts, the attacker gained access via RDP brute force, then escalated privileges (Kerberos ticket, SeDebugPrivilege) and executed a Base64-encoded PowerShell command flagged as a suspicious decoded payload — consistent with post-compromise tooling being staged on the host.

Case 03

Email Header & Phishing Analysis

MXToolbox
Scenario

Verifying whether an email's claimed sending domain could be trusted, or whether it showed signs of spoofing commonly used in phishing campaigns.

Method

Ran the email header through MXToolbox to check SPF record validity and alignment, then reviewed DMARC policy enforcement.

1/3
Header Analyzed overview — MXToolbox delivery information summary
SPF checks — record published, valid syntax, domain alignment confirmed
DMARC checks — policy set to quarantine/reject, external validation passed
← swipe for 3 images →
Finding

SPF and DMARC were both correctly configured and enforcing a quarantine/reject policy — meaning spoofed emails claiming to be from this domain would be rejected or flagged rather than reaching an inbox unchallenged.

Case 04

Network Reconnaissance with Nmap

Nmap TryHackMe — DVWA
Scenario

Practicing the reconnaissance phase of a penetration test against a deliberately vulnerable target machine (TryHackMe's DVWA room).

Method

Ran an Nmap scan against the target IP to enumerate open ports and identify running services before further investigation.

TryHackMe room view — target machine details (IP, expiry) alongside the live terminal running the scan
Finding

Identified an open SSH service with enumerable host keys, and an HTTP service hosting a DVWA login page with a missing HttpOnly flag on its session cookie and a disallowed entry in robots.txt — both worth flagging in a real assessment as configuration weaknesses.

Case 05

Endpoint Security & SOC Dashboard Monitoring

SOC Dashboard Windows Event Logs EDR monitoring
Scenario

Explored a SOC dashboard tool for endpoint detection and response (EDR) monitoring, covering fleet health and Windows Event Log correlation across a simulated domain.

Method

Reviewed endpoint status across the monitored domain, then drilled into Windows Event Logs for a specific host to inspect logon activity and event severity.

1/2
Endpoint Security overview — 45 monitored Windows endpoints, all reporting healthy
Windows Event Logs — DC-01 host, showing a successful logon (4624) alongside repeated failed logon attempts (4625) across multiple accounts
← swipe for 2 images →
Finding

The event log for DC-01 showed a pattern consistent with a password-guessing attempt — a single successful logon (Event ID 4624) preceded by a run of failed logons (Event ID 4625) against different usernames in quick succession, worth escalating for follow-up investigation.

Case 06

Phishing URL Verification with VirusTotal

VirusTotal URL reputation analysis
Scenario

A link styled as an airline booking page required assessment to determine whether it was legitimate, malicious, or suspicious before being trusted or acted upon.

Method

Submitted the URL to VirusTotal to scan it against 92 security vendors and threat intelligence sources, with the goal of classifying the link as legitimate, malicious, or suspicious based on vendor consensus, delivery metadata, and content type.

1/2
VirusTotal URL report — flyairpeace.com/book-a-flight/, 0/92 vendor detections
Security vendors' analysis — full vendor list returning Clean status
← swipe for 2 images →
Finding

All 92 vendors classified the URL as Clean, with no red flags in delivery status or content type — a result that indicates the link is likely safe to proceed with. That said, a Clean verdict from VirusTotal is an indicator, not a guarantee: vendor databases can lag behind newly registered or low-traffic domains that haven't yet been flagged. For that reason, a clean scan should be treated as one data point in the assessment, and paired with manual review of the domain and page content before a URL is fully trusted.
